params.label: A chain of commits, each pointing back to the one before

items.question: Tap every commit that could have brought in the bug.

feedback.correct: 6, 7 or 8: everything after the last good commit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every commit after the last good one, up to the broken one.

byKey.not-eight: You left out commit 8. The bug may have arrived in 8 itself.
byKey.with-five: Commit 5 ran fine, so the bug was not in it yet.

explain.text: Commit 5 works, so the bug arrived after it: in 6, 7 or 8. Commit 8 is a suspect too. Running commit 7 next would settle it in at most two runs.

items.prose:
You wrote a new file, `signal.py`, and edited `backtest.py`. Then you run:

```sh
$ git add signal.py
$ git commit -m "Add 20-day signal"
```

params.label: Working folder, staging area and repository

state.caption: Each card is a change to a file. The files themselves stay in your working folder.

items.question: Drag each change to where it is afterwards.

feedback.correct: Only the staged file was committed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A commit takes only what was staged.

byKey.bt: backtest.py was never staged, so the commit left it in the working folder.
byKey.sig: signal.py was staged and then committed, so it is in the repository.

explain.text: `git add signal.py` staged the new file and the commit recorded it. The edit to backtest.py was never staged, so it is still waiting in the working folder.

items.prose: The versions in your project right now:
items.question: Which lines appear in `git status`? Select all that apply.

options.why: costs.py is v2 in the folder and v2 staged. Nothing about it is unstaged.
signal.py is in the last commit, so it is tracked. It matches everywhere, so it is not listed at all.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare staged with committed, then working with staged.

items.prose: `git diff` prints this for an edit to the costs in `backtest.py`:
items.question: Tap every line the edit added to the file.

feedback.correct: Two lines were added: the cost and the new P&L line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the plus lines below the @@ header.

byKey.header: You included `+++ b/backtest.py`. That is a header naming the new version of the file, not an added line.
byKey.r1c0: `+++ b/backtest.py` is a header naming the new version of the file.
byKey.r4c0: This line starts with a minus: it was removed.

explain.text: The `---` and `+++` lines name the old and new file; the changes start after `@@`. Two plus lines were added and one minus line removed. The cost per trade doubled from 5 bp to 10 bp.

items.prose: Last week you committed `prices.csv` by mistake. Today you add the line `prices.csv` to `.gitignore`, then download fresh prices into the file.
items.question: What does `git status` say about `prices.csv`?

options.text: Changes not staged for commit: modified: `prices.csv`
Nothing: the file is ignored now
options.why: You expected .gitignore to cover every file. It only hides untracked files; a committed file stays tracked.
The file is in a commit, so Git tracks it. It cannot be untracked.

options.text: It is deleted from the repository
options.why: Ignoring a file never deletes it. You would have to remove it from tracking yourself.

feedback.correct: Ignoring does not apply to a file Git already tracks.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether Git tracks the file already.

byKey.nothing: You expected the new line to hide the file. .gitignore only affects untracked files.

explain.text: .gitignore only stops untracked files from showing up. prices.csv is in a commit, so Git keeps tracking it and reports the change. `git rm --cached prices.csv` stops tracking it; level 3 covers that.

items.prose: You changed the backtest to trade at the next day's open instead of today's close, and staged it.
items.question: Which commit message is best?

options.text: Trade at the next day's open instead of today's close

options.why: Git records the file already. The message should say what changed.
This could describe any commit. You could not find it in the log.
Work in progress says nothing about the change.

feedback.correct: It says what changed, in a form you can find in the log.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the message you could find later.

explain.text: A message should say what the commit changes, starting with a verb. Scanning `git log --oneline` for open or close finds this one at once.

items.prose: You staged a broken edit to `plot.py`. You want the staging area and your file both back as they were in the last commit, then to check.
items.question: Put the commands in order.

feedback.correct: Unstage first, then restore the file, then check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. While the broken edit is staged, plain restore copies the broken staged version.

explain.text: `git restore --staged` puts the last commit's version back in the staging area. Then plain `git restore` copies that over your file. In the other order, the file is restored from the broken staged copy, so nothing changes.

items.prose:
In a repository with nothing staged, you run:

```sh
$ git add a.py
$ git commit -m "One"
$ # edit a.py and save
$ git commit -m "Two"
$ git add a.py
$ git commit -m "Three"
```
items.question: How many new commits are in the history?

feedback.correct: Two. The commit "Two" found nothing staged.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check what is staged before each commit.

byKey.three: You counted "Two". The edit was saved but not staged, so that commit was refused.
byKey.four: You counted the save as a snapshot too. Saves never reach the history.

explain.text: "One" committed the staged a.py. The edit before "Two" was never staged, so that commit was refused. After `git add`, "Three" recorded the edit.
